content.thinking:
I'm pulling together the postmortem on the HighLatency alert for io-shop: p95 latency climbed sharply during the incident while errors stayed at their normal level. There were no deploys or flag changes around then, and the replica count read 3 at T10.1. I'm weighing the autoscaler flapping between 3 and 6 as a candidate cause, and I want to check what the rows actually show before I accept it.

Now I'm checking whether the autoscaler flapping actually shows up in the rows, since so far it's only a candidate. The record says raising the replica floor from 3 to 6 is what fixed it, and the values file has scale-down stabilization set to 0, though nothing confirms that ran. I'm also noting that the account-page client disconnects began before the onset, so they don't clearly line up with the latency rise.

I'm checking whether the 3-replica capacity shortfall holds up, since the mitigation of raising the floor to 6 confirmed it. Then I'm ruling out recent deploys and flag changes, though nothing was found in that window, so it means none came back rather than ruling out an earlier change. The step I'm stuck on is the trigger, since there's no change to tie to it, so I'll attach the ruled-out checks to the capacity step.

I'm checking whether the autoscaler could drop straight back to the floor of 3 after scaling up, since the values file sets scale-down stabilization to 0 (F1). That's the mechanism I'd need to tie the flapping to the capacity shortfall, and I still have to confirm the replica counts actually alternated.

I'm settling on the root cause: the production values file sets scale-down stabilization to 0, so the autoscaler could drop from 6 back to 3 replicas, and at 3 the service fell behind and p95 latency climbed. Since no row shows the flapping itself and that reading of F1 never actually ran, this rests on an unverified mechanism.

I'm now setting out the causal chain for the postmortem, with the last step tying the replica shortfall to the production autoscaler's zero scale-down stabilization, since no change in the record marks the trigger.

I'm settling the second step of the chain: the service was short on replicas, and raising the floor from 3 to 6 brought latency back and stopped the alert. I'm also noting that at the 3-replica reading, every replica ran the same revision, so a bad release isn't the explanation there.

I'm settling the third step of the chain: the autoscaler probably fell back to its floor of replicas right after scaling up, since the production values file sets the scale-down stabilization window to zero (F1). I still need to confirm that the replica counts actually alternated.

I'm now drafting the last part of the postmortem: the scale-down stabilization window of zero in the production values file is the final step of the chain, but the record doesn't show why it was set that way. I also need a contributing factor on the missing check, so I'm proposing a CI policy that validates autoscaler stabilization windows across services before deploy. There's a second contributing factor forming too, that the alert wasn't linked to an on-call incident, which I'm still working out.

I'm weighing whether the missing page belongs as a contributing factor or as something that went wrong; it's a condition from before the incident, around how the alert was routed, so I'll list it under what went wrong, with an action item to route HighLatency alerts on io-shop to on-call paging. I'm also starting to think about a third possible contributing factor, the autoscaler's floor of 3 as a safeguard, but I haven't settled that yet.

I'm noting that the replica-churn idea has no alert behind it: nothing paged on the autoscaler swinging between counts, so the latency alert was the only thing that caught the fault. I'm not sure the alternation is actually shown in the rows yet, so I'll leave it as a question for now.

I'm drafting the action items for the postmortem: a CI check that validates scale-down stabilization windows across every deploy values file, an alert on io-shop's replica count oscillating, and routing the io-shop HighLatency alert to on-call paging. I'm also noting that the hand-raised replica floor only holds latency down until something resets it, since the stabilization window was still set to zero.

Now I'm moving on to the lessons section, starting with what went well, where the investigator agent's reads of metrics, changes, logs and flags are the first item.

Now I'm listing the lessons, starting with what went well: the Investigator Agent formed candidate causes from the metrics, changes, logs and flags, Argus ruled out a flag change, the Mitigation Agent raised the autoscaler floor as a reversible step, and the Code-Fix Agent proposed a draft fix PR with a test.

I'm noting that the replica count swinging between 3 and 6 isn't actually shown in any row, since it rests on the Investigator's candidate and Code-Fix's reading of the values file. I also have to assume the configuration Code-Fix read is what the running revision used, because the rollout history doesn't name that revision.

I'm checking the rest of the postmortem draft: the latency step's wording, the contributing factors, and whether the zero stabilization window's history is known. The symptom and first causal step are phrased plainly enough to stand as written.

I'm settling how to word the slowdown in plain terms: the slowest requests got much slower, and I'll avoid putting any percentile label or number in the text.

action_items.item: Add a CI policy check that fails any service's deploy values whose autoscaler scale-down stabilization window is missing or set too low, so the check covers every change like this one and not only io-shop's own test.
Add an alert for when io-shop's autoscaler keeps moving the replica count up and down over a short stretch.
Route the HighLatency alert on io-shop to the on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers had to wait much longer than usual for io-shop's slowest requests to finish, while the share of failed requests stayed within its normal variation.

ruled_out.what: A deploy, release or flag change on the service setting it off: no production change came back for the day before the onset, and the flag provider showed no flag change by anyone but Argus in the hour it read. No change was found that set the incident off, and no earlier change was ruled out by the service being measured healthy with it in place.

causal_chain.step: io-shop had too few replicas serving it for the load it was under. When the Investigator read the rollout at {T10.1}, all {T10.2} replicas were running a single revision.
The autoscaler likely dropped back to its floor of {F1.6} replicas right after each scale-up, since the production values file sets its scale-down stabilization window to {F1.3}.

input.cause_in_plain_words: The shop's automatic scaling likely kept taking away the extra servers it had just added, which left too few servers to answer shoppers quickly.

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that would stop an autoscaler setting with a zero scale-down stabilization window from reaching production.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The setting would have been rejected before it went out, so the autoscaler would have held its added replicas and the service would not have slowed down.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No alert on the autoscaler moving io-shop's replica count back and forth was seen. The fault was found only by the latency alert.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The flapping capacity could have been caught when it began, instead of only after the slow responses had held long enough to fire the latency rule.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent formed its candidate causes after reading the service's metrics, production changes, rollout state and log lines.
Argus read the flag provider's history and found no flag change by anyone else.
The Mitigation Agent raised io-shop's autoscaler floor, an action that can be put back.
The Mitigation Agent checked the service and judged the action confirmed once the alerting rule had stopped firing.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix with a new test as draft pull request #536, for a person to review.

went_wrong: Nobody was paged: the alert was not linked to any on-call incident.

input.root_cause: The production autoscaler settings for io-shop set the scale-down stabilization window to {F1.3}, so the controller acts on the lower CPU per replica that its own scale-up to {F1.5} replicas produced, drops straight back to {F1.6}, and at that count CPU per replica climbs past its {F1.7} target and requests queue, which drives response times up until it scales up again.
input.still_at_risk: io-shop's pages could slow down again in the same way if its autoscaler floor goes back to {T22.2} replicas while the scale-down setting in its repository is still unchanged.
input.symptom: Shop pages slowed down for shoppers
